Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**The Court May Consider [the Agreement] Without Converting This Motion into One for Summary Judgment.**

Review under Rule 12(b)(6) generally reaches the allegations of the complaint, attached exhibits, and matters properly subject to judicial notice. *Swartz v. KPMG LLP*, 476 F.3d 756, 763 (9th Cir. 2007) (per curiam). It also reaches documents incorporated by reference, which a court may consider "without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003).

A document need not be attached to the complaint to be incorporated into it. It is enough that "the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Id.* A defendant may offer such a document, and the court may treat it as part of the complaint and "may assume that its contents are true for purposes of a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6)." *Id.*; *see also Davis v. HSBC Bank Nev., N.A.*, 691 F.3d 1152, 1160 (9th Cir. 2012). Courts likewise may consider documents whose contents are alleged in the complaint and whose authenticity no party questions. *Branch v. Tunnell*, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119 (9th Cir. 2002); *see Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006) (permitting consideration where the complaint refers to the document, the document is central to the claim, and no party questions the copy's authenticity).

Nor can a plaintiff avoid the doctrine by declining to quote or describe a document's terms. Incorporation extends to situations in which the claim depends on a document's contents, the defendant attaches it to the motion, and the parties do not dispute its authenticity, even though the complaint does not explicitly allege those contents. *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005); *see Parrino v. FHP, Inc.*, 146 F.3d 699, 706 (9th Cir. 1998) (refusing to let a plaintiff defeat dismissal by deliberately omitting documents on which the claims depend), *superseded by statute on other grounds as stated in Abrego Abrego v. Dow Chem. Co.*, 443 F.3d 676 (9th Cir. 2006). The doctrine thus "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018).

Once a document is properly before the court, the plaintiff's characterization of it does not control. A court need not accept as true allegations contradicted by exhibits or judicially noticeable matter. *Sprewell v. Golden State Warriors*, 266 F.3d 979, 988 (9th Cir.), *amended on denial of reh'g*, 275 F.3d 1187 (9th Cir. 2001); *Daniels-Hall v. Nat'l Educ. Ass'n*, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010). The same logic applies to an incorporated document, whose contents the court may assume to be true. *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908.

[The Agreement] satisfies these standards. The Complaint refers to it [repeatedly], and Plaintiff's [claim] depends on its terms: Plaintiff cannot establish [the alleged duty and breach] without it. [Compl. ¶¶ __.] Defendant has attached a true and correct copy as Exhibit [A], and its authenticity cannot reasonably be disputed. Defendant therefore does not seek to inject a document merely mentioned in passing, or to use one simply to dispute well-pleaded facts. *See Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908–09; *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002–03. Rather, Defendant relies on [identify the dispositive provision], which Plaintiff's own claim places at issue. The Court should consider Exhibit [A] in full and decide this motion under Rule 12(b)(6), without converting it into a motion for summary judgment under Rule 12(d).
